questions.question: Compare capitalism and communism as economic and political systems.
questions.expected_answer: Capitalism: private ownership of the means of production, production for profit, prices set by free-market competition; in the US linked with liberal democracy, multi-party elections and individual freedoms; criticised for inequality and depressions. Communism: based on Marx and Engels (Communist Manifesto, 1848); in the Soviet Union after 1917, state ownership and central planning (five-year plans), promising equality, jobs, free education and health care; in practice a one-party state under Stalin with the Gulag, famines and restricted freedoms.

questions.question: Explain why tension grew between the Allies in 1945, referring to the Yalta and Potsdam conferences.
questions.expected_answer: The alliance was a marriage of convenience against Germany; mistrust stemmed from Western intervention in Russia 1918-20, appeasement, the Nazi-Soviet Pact, the delayed second front and the secret atomic bomb. Yalta (February 1945; Roosevelt, Churchill, Stalin) agreed on German zones, UN, Soviet entry against Japan and free elections, but disagreed over Poland. At Potsdam (July-August 1945) Truman and Attlee replaced Roosevelt and Churchill, the Red Army occupied Eastern Europe, Truman revealed the bomb, and they argued over reparations and Poland.

questions.question: Explain how Soviet control of Eastern Europe and the American policy of containment divided Europe by 1947-1949.
questions.expected_answer: Seeking security after losing about 27 million people, Stalin backed communist takeovers in Poland, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and Czechoslovakia (1948) through rigged elections and pressure, creating satellite states. Churchill's Iron Curtain speech (5 March 1946) and Kennan's Long Telegram shaped Western views. The US adopted containment: the Truman Doctrine (12 March 1947, aid to Greece and Turkey) and the Marshall Plan (about 13 billion dollars, 1948-1952). The USSR banned satellites from the plan and created Cominform (1947) and Comecon (1949).
